Twenty-five comments

“Ye Banks And Braes O’ Bonnie Doon” in 6/8

Key signature: G Major
Submitted on January 5th 2007 by nicholas.
https://thesession.org/tunes/6599

The transcription here is based on a few different takes. We used to play it all on its own and just change keys, so I’ve given a sample of that here, from G Major to D Major, and we’d finish were we started, for example G… It is nice to play one tune on its own, without feeling obliged to set it up in a string of other things, to get familiar with it as this would allow, in more than one key… Waltzes work well that way, as the dancers get to also become familiar with the melody, and hearing someone humming it later is an extra prize for the musicians…it has sunk in and made a place for itself in someone else…

I hope this is ‘different’ enough, as a waltz and in treatment and optional variations, to survive, and good if that’s so. You will find a straight variation in 3/4 in the ‘comments’ for the 6/8 linked to above. There are some other 6/8 takes on this melody and I’ll try to add one or two to the ‘comments’ for the 6/8 version…

I’ve heard some great renditions of this air, and maybe, hoping, again if this survives, some of those other 3/4 versions will be transcribed and added here… Shmaltz, I know, but I love it ~ as a musician, dancer and raconteur (someone else’s accusation)… ;-)

Re: Ye Banks And Braes

Everyone probably already knows this, but this is the melody to Robert Burns’ song Ye Banks and Braes of Bonny Doon, which is more or less about the narrator being heartbroken, wondering why the birds are singing so happily when he is so sad. It’s a beautiful set of lyrics and I recommend reading them (or better yet, listening to them).

Re: Ye Banks And Braes < Kennet’s dream

John Purser, of Carnyx fame, who prepared the notes for the CD ‘Forever Fortune’ (Scottish music in the 18th Century), reckons that he has found the earliest if not the original version of the melody Burns used for his ‘Ye banks and braes…’
It is to be found in James Oswald’s Caledonian Pocket Companion (published in the 1750’s)
(p.106 in the 12 vol. edition) under the name Kennet’s Dream, “which refers to Alexander Bruce of Kennet House in Clackmannanshire.”
You can see the score for yourself here:
https://archive.org/details/caledonianpocket00stua/page/106/mode/1up
N.B.: This score actually works more like a grid since the fiddle is to be tuned in scordatura, as indicated by the chord at the head of the stave.
The slow tune is followed by several ‘brisk’ variations as is still commonly practiced in Scotland in the piping world.
I will post a non scordatura version here in due time so that non fiddlers can read it easily.

↳ Posted by birlibirdie on January 25th, 2024.

Kennet’s dream, X:7

Robert Burns owned a coppy of James Oswald’s Caledonian Pocket Companion (London, 1750’s). Kennet’s dream is thought to be the original tune the bard set his song ‘Ye Banks and Braes’ to. Several pointers lead John Purser to believe it is an Oswald composition, theme and variations included.
The fiddle is tuned c#-A-E-A, instead of e-A-D-G, to allow full harmonic resonance.
In the original edition, the c#’s in the score are double-stopped and several long notes are trilled.
See comments above for more details.

↳ Posted by birlibirdie on January 27th, 2024.

Re: Ye Banks and Braes / Kennet’s Dream (family of tunes)

From this Scottish origin (perhaps wholy Oswaldian), this tune branched out into a family of melodies mostly found today in the USA.
For the record, a few other names are given here, an A to Z list which is no way exhaustive:

(mind that some of the names come from songs that exist in a variety of settings)

I’m a rambler and a gambler (USA)
J‘ai fait l’amour chez l’Onc Bab (Louisiana,) = Une once de tabac
Jubilee (USA) <more loosely related>
Kennet’s dream (J. Oswald, Scotland, c.1750)
Pretty boy Floyd (a 4/4 loose connection, penned by Woodie Guthrie)
Pretty Mary (USA)
Rye Whisky / Rye Whiskey (USA)
Wagoners lad / Waggoner’s lad (USA)
Ye banks and braes of Bonny Doon (words by Robbie Burns; the 1st musical phrase is rather different but the rest is unmistakable)
…
The list goes on.
The tune is still sprouting new verses and even entire new songs. Wagoner’s lad (of which several versions exist) was translated in French as Le fils du roulier (“Mes chevaux n’ont plus faim”) by the late Graeme Allwright (R.I.P.) for example.
Oswald may have been inspired himself by other popular tunes. Part 2 of his piece shares strands with the shanty ‘Blow the man down’, for instance which melody may have long predated its 19th century(?) lyric.

The Poor Stranger, X:8

The Poor Stranger

1.
As I went a-walking one morning in spring
to hear the birds whistle and the nightingales sing
I heard a fair maiden and sad was her moan
-oh i’m a poor stranger and far from my home
2.
I’ll build my love a cottage at the edge of this town
where the Lords, Dukes and Earls they will not knock it down
And if the boys ask her why she lives alone
she’ll say she’s a stranger and far from her home.

source;
Bill Meek / Ossian publications Ltd.

These two verses and the tune have also appeared in print in Kodály Society teaching books.

Re: Ye Banks And Braes

To answer your question, Bazza, Come by the hills, The poor stranger, Ye banks and braes seem to be ultimately derived or related to Kenneth’s dream as explained above (5 months ago).
A dolphin is more like a shark than a bat but the 2 mammals share an internal body plan and common ancestor which make them belong together.
Trying to sort tunes -or any object- in any particular order will always leave items out, that do not entirely fit in one or the other categories:
None of the tunes above are commonly heard in itm sessions and all are known, under a variety of names, in many different versions and hybrids; I chose to post X:7 and X:8 here, cause I believe it is historically pertinent and lyrical congruent to do so, rather than for their melodic similarity (at a glance) but I understand -and share- the hesitation.
